tool.name: FTIR and Raman spectrometers
tool.measures: the chemical bonds of the stone (infrared) and the signature of its crystal lattice (Raman)
tips: Clean the stone before analysing it
Read the peaks, not the general shape

steps.title: Going further than visible light
steps.text: The instruments of the basic laboratory use visible light. To go further, more expensive instruments are used, which analyse the very material of the stone, without destroying it.

steps.title: Infrared (FTIR)
steps.text: The FTIR spectrometer (Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy) sends infrared light onto the stone. Each type of chemical bond (O–H, C–H...) absorbs at a precise wavelength and leaves a peak in the spectrum. It is the instrument for treatments: it reveals oil or resin in the cracks of an emerald, the polymer in a jade, the water in an opal. Epoxy resin is however hard to spot.

steps.title: Raman
steps.text: The Raman spectrometer lights the stone with a laser and measures how the light is scattered. The way the crystal lattice vibrates gives each mineral a unique signature, even for a very small inclusion. It identifies the stone with certainty (quartz, beryl, corundum...), and even the inclusion it carries: it thus helps separate a natural growth from a synthesis.

steps.title: The electron microscope (SEM)
steps.text: The SEM (scanning electron microscope) magnifies thousands of times. It shows the growth structures at the microscopic scale: a natural stone and a laboratory stone do not grow the same way, and the SEM shows it. It is a laboratory examination, long and expensive, kept for difficult cases.

steps.title: To remember
steps.text: • FTIR: chemical bonds, so treatments (oil, resin) and water. • Raman: the exact identity of the mineral and of its inclusions. • SEM: the growth structure, natural or synthetic. • These instruments confirm what simple instruments leave you suspecting.
